title: Getting Fitter Makes You Mentally Stronger Too
excerpt: Getting fitter has changed more than my body. The discipline of training, learning to do things when I don't feel like it and becoming more comfortable with discomfort has changed how I approach difficult things outside the gym too.
content:
One of the things I've started to realise since getting into better shape is that the biggest changes haven't necessarily been physical.

The physical stuff is obviously the easiest to notice. I'm stronger, I look better, my clothes fit differently and I generally feel healthier. Those are the things I wanted from getting fitter in the first place, so I'm certainly not complaining. But somewhere along the way, something has changed mentally as well. I'm a little more comfortable doing difficult things, a little more willing to get on with things when I don't feel like it, and, perhaps most importantly, a little more confident that I can stick to something once I've decided to do it.

I don't think going to the gym magically makes you mentally stronger. It's probably much simpler than that. Training gives you a regular chance to practise some behaviours that happen to be useful in the rest of your life too.

## Learning to do things when you don't feel like it

Anyone who exercises regularly will know that motivation isn't particularly reliable. There are days when you really want to train and everything feels easy, and plenty of others when you've had a rubbish day, you're tired, you've slept badly or you'd simply rather sit on the sofa. I've had plenty of those myself. The interesting thing is that once exercise becomes part of your routine, you gradually stop treating motivation as a requirement. Sometimes you still don't want to go, but you go anyway.

That sounds fairly insignificant, but I think it's one of the most useful lessons I've picked up from getting fitter. You don't always need to feel ready before you act. Sometimes you just need to start. Once you've experienced that often enough, the same idea starts to creep into other parts of your life: jobs at work you don't particularly want to do, things around the house you've been putting off, personal projects that are much easier to postpone than to start. You don't suddenly become hugely disciplined, but you get a little more comfortable with the idea that *not wanting to do something* isn't necessarily a good enough reason not to do it.

## Getting comfortable with discomfort

Exercise has also changed the way I think about discomfort. I'm not talking about ignoring pain or pushing through an injury, because there's an important difference between something being painful and something simply being difficult. I mean that feeling when you've got a few reps left and your muscles are burning, or when you're halfway through a workout, tired, and would quite happily stop. It's uncomfortable, but it's temporary, and learning that distinction has been useful for me.

You start to realise that discomfort isn't always a warning sign telling you to stop. Sometimes it's just what doing something difficult feels like. You can admit you don't particularly enjoy it without immediately deciding you need to escape it. I think that's a useful mindset outside the gym as well. Difficult conversations, challenging work, learning something you're not good at and taking on something outside your comfort zone can all feel uncomfortable. That doesn't automatically mean you've made the wrong decision. Sometimes it just means you've chosen something that takes effort.

## Building trust in yourself

Perhaps the biggest change, though, has been my relationship with my own commitments. Every time I decide I'm going to train and then turn up, I'm keeping a small promise to myself. It doesn't have to be a brilliant workout, or even a particularly enjoyable one. What matters is that I said I'd do something and then followed through.

One workout obviously doesn't change very much, but hundreds of those small decisions start to add up. You begin to have evidence that you can rely on yourself, which is quite different from telling yourself you're going to be more disciplined or make some big change from Monday. You said you were going to train and you trained. You said you'd go for a walk and you went. You decided to improve your diet and stuck with it for another week. None of those things is particularly impressive on its own, but together they can change how you see yourself.

I think that has done more for my confidence than I expected. For me, confidence has turned out to be less about believing everything will work out and more about knowing that if something is difficult, I'll have a go at dealing with it instead of immediately looking for a way out.

## And then there are the obvious mental benefits

There are also the more straightforward benefits of exercising regularly. I generally feel better after I've trained. I feel more switched on, my head feels clearer and I tend to have more energy. I'm often less stressed too, which makes everything else seem a little easier. Work feels more manageable, I'm more likely to be productive and I'm less inclined to spend an evening sitting around overthinking things.

It's hard to separate all of this neatly, because your body and your mind aren't two completely separate systems. If you're moving more, sleeping better, eating reasonably well and getting stronger, it would be surprising if none of that affected how you feel. That's one of the things I appreciate most about fitness now. The workout might only take half an hour, but the way I feel afterwards can shape the rest of the day.

## It's about more than getting fit

That's why fitness has gradually become about much more than getting into shape for me. The physical changes still matter, and they're probably what got me started, but they've turned out to be only part of the benefit. The bigger change has been what I've learned about doing things consistently, dealing with discomfort and following through when the motivation isn't there.

I'm certainly not suddenly some hugely disciplined person. I still have days when I can't be bothered and days when I choose the easy option. But I think that's the point. Getting fitter hasn't removed those feelings. It's given me somewhere to practise dealing with them.

Every workout is another chance to show up, do something difficult and keep a promise to myself. Do that often enough and it starts to change how you approach other challenges too, because you've proved to yourself again and again that you can handle difficult things. The gym builds a stronger, fitter body, and alongside it a habit of showing up and carrying on when things get hard, which turns out to be useful just about everywhere else.
